conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad you’re here—adjusting to new motherhood can feel like riding an emotional wave, and it’s brave to check in on how you’re doing.

Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s simply a snapshot of your mood and anxiety so we can make sure you have the right support.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team. If any question feels hard, we can pause or come back to it—this is a safe space, and you’re in control.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no clipboard, no jargon. When you answer, just tell me what feels true for you; there are no right or wrong responses.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Hi, Maya… thanks for having me.  
I still get little sparks of enjoyment—like when the baby grips my finger or when I manage a hot shower—but it’s definitely duller. Things that used to feel exciting, like texting friends or baking, just feel… flat. I’ll do them, but it’s more going through the motions than actually feeling happy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a silly face or when the dog does something goofy—but it’s not the same easy, belly laugh I used to have. It feels kind of forced or fades quickly, and then I’m right back to feeling kind of numb or tired.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I’ll tell myself, “Tomorrow I’ll feel excited about coffee with my mom,” but when the time comes it just feels… meh. Even little plans—like ordering take-out or putting on a new show—don’t give me that buzz they used to. I still do them, mostly to break up the day, but the looking-forward part feels flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it must be something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. When I couldn’t get him to nap yesterday, I kept replaying it, telling myself a “good mom” would’ve figured it out. My head knows it’s not all on me, but the thought still pops up and sits heavy for a while.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes. Like, I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds weird in the middle of the night, even though he’s fine, and then I’m lying there wide-awake listening. It usually passes pretty fast—I can tell myself he’s okay—but those random spikes of worry still hit out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had full panic, but there’ve been moments—mostly when I’m alone with him—where my chest tightens and I think, “What if I’m not doing enough?” It’s like a quick rush of fear, then it fades. Nothing I can point to, just a sudden wave of “what if something goes wrong?” and then I’m back to normal.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the dishes pile up or he won’t settle, I feel like I’m juggling too many balls and they’re all about to drop. I usually manage to push through, but it’s that tight-chest feeling of “how am I going to get everything done?”—especially by late afternoon.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I get pretty exhausted, so once I finally lie down I’m out. Sometimes it takes me a little while to drift off—my mind will circle around tomorrow’s to-dos—but I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep. I’m mostly just tired and glad to rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like a little gray cloud that follows me around—but it’s not constant. It hits hardest in the late afternoon or when I’m feeding him alone and the house is quiet. I wouldn’t call it miserable, more like a steady ache that comes and goes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… this past week it’s happened maybe twice. Once was when he wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch, and the tears just welled up before I could stop them. The other time was after a short text from my best friend—totally harmless—but it felt like I was failing at everything. Each bout lasted a few minutes, then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and low, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I want to be here for my baby, even on the rough days.

You've shared that the sparkle has dimmed: activities you used to anticipate now feel flat, laughter is muted, and a steady "gray cloud" of sadness drifts in-especially during quiet afternoon feeds. You worry about being "enough" for your baby, blame yourself when he fusses, and sometimes feel a sudden tight-chest wave of fear, yet you summon the energy to push through each day. It's clear you love your son deeply and want to be well for him, and you've courageously reached out to understand why joy feels so elusive right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can still laugh occasionally but describes it as forced, fleeting, and diminished from her baseline, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes almost complete loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent self-blame that intrudes and lingers, clearly matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, unprovoked worry spikes several times daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden chest-tightening fear that appears without clear cause and resolves quickly—best fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent stress and feeling overwhelmed, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "some of the time" with recurring episodes, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 16 falls above the ≥14 cut-off that flags probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core criteria echoed include diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), low mood (<sym>feeling sad</sym>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/guilt (<sym>self-blame</sym>), and recurrent anxiety without clear triggers. Symptoms cluster over the past seven days, cause subjective distress and functional difficulty, and onset is within four weeks postpartum, fitting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. No self-harm items were endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and possible medication evaluation
3. Share results with support partner and identify daily help with infant care and household tasks to protect rest and recovery
4. Begin gentle mood-boosting routines: 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced snacks every 3-4 h, five-minute breathing or mindfulness when baby naps
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track response to interventions and adjust plan as needed
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary (EPDS-based)

Main endorsed symptoms:
- Anhedonia, reduced capacity for pleasure/enjoyment  
- Episodic tearfulness, low mood ("gray cloud," "steady ache")  
- Excessive self-blame, feelings of inadequacy as mother  
- Unprompted worry and situational panic-like sensations (chest tightness, "what-ifs")  
- Afternoon worsening of mood, sense of being overwhelmed

Patterns of clinical interest:
- Persistent mild-to-moderate depressive features with functional impact  
- Anxiety symptoms (generalized worry and brief panic sensations) occurring several times daily  
- Absence of suicidal ideation; no self-harm thoughts reported

Risk factors identified:
✓ Loss of pleasure and anticipatory enjoyment  
✓ Crying spells linked to perceived parenting failure  
✓ Recurrent intrusive worry while infant sleeping  
✓ Tendency toward self-criticism/guilt  
✗ No current suicidal ideation (screen negative)

Screening impression:
Responses place patient above standard cut-off for possible postpartum depression (with comorbid anxiety features). Symptoms present most days, interfere with emotional engagement, but do not presently include safety concerns. Recommend formal clinical assessment and consideration of further evaluation for postpartum mood/anxiety disorder.
